Containers whose values can be transformed while the container keeps its shape: a list's elements, an optional's value, a result's success. The trait ranges over the container type, so a function written once works on any of them:

```kex
let bumped(F is Functor => xs: F<Integer>) -> F<Integer> = xs.map { |x| x + 1 }

bumped([1, 2])     # => [2, 3]
bumped(Just(1))    # => Just(2)
bumped(Ok(1))      # => Ok(2)
```


Containers whose values can be combined with another container's when neither depends on the other. `with` applies a function to the values of both. A list combines every pair. An `Optional` or a `Result` combines the two values or returns the first failure. A `Validation` combines the values or collects every failure, which suits checking several independent inputs.

```kex
[1, 2].with([10, 20]) { |a, b| a + b }       # => [11, 21, 12, 22]
Just(1).with(Just(2)) { |a, b| a + b }       # => Just(3)
name.checked.with(email.checked) do |n, e|
  Signup { name: n, email: e }               # every failed check, or a Signup
end
```

Returns the atom whose name is `text`.

The atom is created if it does not exist yet. On the BEAM atoms are never freed and a node holds at most about a million, so only build atoms from a bounded set of names, such as node names or configuration keys. For untrusted input use `text.to(Atom)`, which only finds existing atoms.

Named constants such as `:ok`, `:error` and `:reset`, used for labels, statuses and message tags.

Atoms with the same name are equal, and an atom never equals a string.

```kex
:ok == :ok                    # => true
:ok == :error                 # => false
:ok.string                    # => "ok"
```

An atom is written with a leading colon. The name may include `@`, as node names do; quote a name that contains spaces or other punctuation:

```kex
:app@localhost
:"app@host.example.com"
:"two words"
```

To convert text to an atom:

```kex
"hello".as(Atom)    # a string literal, converted at compile time
Atom.from("hello")  # creates the atom at run time if it does not exist
"hello".to(Atom)    # Just(:hello) if the atom exists, otherwise None
```

On the BEAM atoms are never freed, so use `text.to(Atom)` for external input. The interpreter (`kex -R`) has no atom table, and there `to(Atom)` converts any string.

An immutable sequence of bytes, such as a file's contents, an HTTP body or a digest.

`Binary` is the compact storage form; `[Byte]` is the same bytes as a list. On BEAM, `take` and `drop` share the original's storage instead of copying it.

```kex
let data = Binary.fromHex("00686900").try
data.length            # => 4
data.at(1)             # => Just(104)
data.take(2).hex       # => "0068"
data.showValue         # => "#Binary<4 bytes>"
```

The type is opaque, so string functions cannot be run on bytes by mistake. Converting to or from text is always explicit, and `to` returns an optional, since the conversion can fail:

```kex
"árvíz".to(Binary)                  # => Just(#Binary<7 bytes>)
Binary.fromBytes([255]).to(String)  # => None
```

Printing a binary shows only its length. It never shows the bytes, so it cannot leak them, and it cannot fail on bytes that are not text. Use `hex`, `base64` or `to(String)` to see the contents.
The binary with no bytes.

Builds a binary from a list of bytes.

Types that can say whether a value holds anything meaningful.

A value is blank when it has no meaningful content: `None`, an empty or all-whitespace string, an empty collection, or `false`. The meaning follows Rails. One test works across types, so a validation can check every field the same way.

```kex
"".blank?        # => true
"   ".blank?     # => true   (unlike "   ".empty?)
[].blank?        # => true
None.blank?      # => true
"hi".present?    # => true
```

`present?` is the negation, and often reads better:

```kex
fields.all? { |name, value| value.present? }
```

Each type decides what that means: empty or whitespace-only for a string, no elements for a collection, `None` for an optional, `false` for a boolean.

Complex numbers: one value, readable in rectangular or polar terms.

A `Complex` is a point in the plane. In rectangular terms it has a real part `re` and an imaginary part `im`; in polar terms, a distance from the origin `abs` and an angle `arg`. Both views work on every value, and either can build one. Parts may be any `Number`, and angles are in radians.

```kex
using Complex

let z = Complex.from(3, 4)
z.abs            # => 5.0
z.polar          # => (5.0, 0.9272952180016122)
Complex.fromPolar(2, Math.PI / 2).im   # approximately 2.0
```

doc.summary:
Builds a `NumberFormat` from a digit pattern, for `to(String, format)`.

The pattern is checked during compilation, so a bad pattern is a build error.

- `0` is a required digit: `000` pads the integer part to three digits,

```kex
using Regex
```

```kex
  Error(e)    => IO.printError("bad pattern at ${e.position}: ${e.message}")
```

A stream holds the rule for producing its elements, so it can be infinite. Elements are computed only when you ask for them with `take`.

doc.summary:
ERB-style templates: scanning template text into nodes, and filling simple templates at run time.

Nothing here is in scope until `using Template`.

`Template.scan` turns template text into its frontmatter and a flat list of +Node+s: plain text and the four kinds of `<% %>` region. It does not run anything or parse Kex; the text inside a tag is kept as written. `Template.render` fills a template that only substitutes values, from a map. A template with Kex control flow is compiled instead, with `Template.html(Kex.embed(path))` or `Template.text(Kex.embed(path))`.

```kex
using Template

let source = "---\ntitle: Welcome\nparams: [name, library: Bool]\n---\nHi <%= name %>!"
let parsed = Template.scan(source).try
parsed.frontmatter.get("title")    # => Just(Scalar("Welcome"))
parsed.parameters.map { |p| (p.name, p.type) }
# => [("name", ""), ("library", "Bool")]
parsed.nodes                       # => [Text("Hi "), Interpolate("name"), Text("!")]
```

A template file's name puts the extension of what it produces before `.ket`, such as `README.md.ket` or `profile.html.ket`, so an editor can highlight it:

```kex
---
params: [name, library: Bool, dependencies: [Dependency]]
---
# <%= name %>

<% if library %>
A Kex library.
<% else %>
A Kex application.
<% end %>

<% dependencies.map do |dep| %>
- `<%= dep.name %>` ~> <%= dep.version %>
<% end %>
```

## Syntax

```kex
<%= expr %>     inserts the value, HTML-escaped by Template.html and
                Template.render
<%== expr %>    inserts the value without escaping
<% ... %>       Kex control code: if and match arms, block bodies, let
<%# ... %>      a comment, which produces nothing
<%- ... -%>     trims the indentation before the tag and the newline
                after it (see Whitespace below)
<%%             a literal <%, for a template that writes ERB itself
```

## Layouts

A layout is a template that takes the page as a block. The two templates do not refer to each other; the Kex code that calls them puts them together. Insert the block's result with `<%== %>`, since it is already rendered, and already escaped if it came from `Template.html`.

```kex
---
params: [title: String, content: Block<String>]
---
<title><%= title %></title>
<main><%== content() %></main>

let frame = Template.html(Kex.embed("views/layouts/auth.html.ket"))
let form = Template.html(Kex.embed("views/signin.html.ket"))

let signin(email: String) -> String = frame("Sign in") { form(email) }
```

## Whitespace

A `<% %>` or `<%# %>` tag that is alone on its line, with only whitespace around it, removes the whole line from the output, its indentation and newline included. So the template reads the way its output does:

```kex
<% if dependencies.count > 0 %>
## Dependencies
<% end %>

# => "## Dependencies\n", with no blank lines where the tags were
```

The `<%-` and `-%>` markers are for a tag that shares its line with other content, where only the author knows what should be trimmed:

```kex
Total: <%= total %> <%- if pending > 0 %>(<%= pending %> pending)<% end %>
```

An interpolation is never trimmed, even alone on its line. It stands for content, so the whitespace around it is content too:

```kex
<%= greeting %>
<%= name %>

# => "Hi\nAda\n", with both newlines kept
```

## Frontmatter

A template may start with a `---` line, then `key: value` lines, then a closing `---` line before the body. The keys are for whatever reads the template, such as a title or a list of tags, and the scanner reads every key the same way. A value is a plain string or a `[a, b, c]` list.

```kex
---
title: Release notes
tags: [changelog, public]
---
# <%= title %>
```

By convention, a template declares its parameters under `params`, as a list of names, each with an optional `: Type`:

```kex
---
params: [name, library: Bool, dependencies: [Dependency]]
---
# <%= name %>
```

`Parsed.parameters` reads that list and splits each entry at its first colon into a `TemplateParam`. The type stays text: `[Dependency]` is the string `"[Dependency]"`, not a resolved Kex type.

Calls `operation` until it succeeds, returns `done`, or runs out of attempts or sleep time, and returns its last result.

The first call happens at once, and each later one after a wait. Named timing options override that field of `schedule` for this run only.

When the block returns a `Result`, `Ok` stops and `Error` is retried. When it returns `done(value)` or `again(value)`, it decides itself. Use one of the two forms throughout the block. An error raised inside the block is not caught or retried.

Running an operation until it succeeds or a `Schedule` runs out.

`run` calls the block at once. An `Ok` result is returned; an `Error` is retried after a wait, and when the schedule runs out the last error is returned as it is. To choose yourself what to retry, return `again` or `done` from the block.

An HTTP 429 or 503 response is `Ok(response)`, so retrying on a status needs `again`. Only retry a write when repeating it is harmless, for example with an idempotency key. The schedule limits the time spent sleeping, not the time spent in the operation, so give requests their own timeouts.

using Net
using Net.HTTP
let schedule = Retry.Schedule { attempts: 5 }
let outcome = Retry.run(schedule: schedule) do
  let result = HTTP.get("https://api.example.com/inventory")
  match result do
    Error(error) => if error.kind == Timeout || error.kind == Connect
      Retry.again(result)
    else
      Retry.done(result)
    end
    Ok(response) => if [429, 502, 503, 504].contains?(response.status.code)
      Retry.again(result)
    else
      Retry.done(result)
    end
  end
end

  Retry.Done(result) => IO.printLine(result)
  Retry.Again(last) => IO.printLine("retry budget exhausted: ${last}")
end

A first-in-first-out queue.

Nothing here is in scope until `using Data.Queue`.

```kex
using Data.Queue

let q = Queue.from([1, 2, 3])
q.enqueue(4).items    # => [1, 2, 3, 4]
q.peek                # => Just(1)
```

The queue is two lists. `front` holds the elements next in line, and `back` holds the newest ones in reverse. `enqueue` adds to the head of `back`, and `dequeue` takes the head of `front`, reversing `back` into `front` when `front` runs out. Both run in amortized constant time.

Stand-ins for the socket capabilities, for testing how code handles a failure.

They are here, not in `mock.kex`, because only code compiled together with this module can implement its capabilities.

TCP, UDP and Unix-domain sockets, and TLS client connections.

Every socket is owned by a process of its own. Functions that can fail return a `NetError`, and closing a socket twice is harmless. Without a timeout argument, accepting and receiving give up after 30 seconds with a `Timeout` error.

Sockets work on BEAM only. On the tree-walking interpreter every operation returns an `UnsupportedBackend` error unless the capability is replaced with a mock such as `Mock.TCP`.

```kex
using Net
using Net.Socket

let listener = TCP.listen(TCP.Endpoint.loopback(Port.from(0).try)).try
let address = listener.localAddress.try
let client = TCP.connect(address).try
client.sendAll("ping".to(Binary).try).try
listener.close
```

A server's answer to a `Handshake`.

`Accept(handler, headers, subprotocol)` sends the 101 response and then runs `handler` with the server `Connection`; its return value is ignored. The `headers` are added to the 101 response, except `Upgrade`, `Connection`, `Sec-WebSocket-Accept`, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` and `Content-Length`, which are dropped. `subprotocol` must be one the client offered, or `None`; choosing any other makes the server answer 500.

`Reject(response)` sends `response` as a plain HTTP response, such as `Response.text(426, "chat.v2 required")` for a client that lacks a subprotocol you need.

There are two families of units: `KB` is 1000 bytes and `KiB` is 1024. Every size is counted in bytes, so the two convert into each other: `1.gibibyte.convertTo(MiB)` gives 1024 MiB.

The constructors have singular names, as in `Units.SI`: `5.megabyte`, `2.mebibyte`. `byteSize` is another name for `byte`.

File and payload functions return plain integer byte counts. Wrap a count with `byte` to convert or display it:

```kex

Binary.fromBytes([104, 105]).length.byte.to(String)  # => Just("2.0 B")

```

```kex
1048576 <= 1.mebibyte    # => true
```

Quantities whose units are built at run time.

`Measure` (units.kex) checks dimensions at compile time. Here a unit is a value: a scale to its dimension's canonical unit, a `Dimension` and a notation. Arithmetic checks dimensions when it runs and returns a `Result`, with `DimensionMismatch` when they do not agree.

```kex
let meters = unit(1.0, Dimensions.base(Length {}), "m").try
let seconds = unit(1.0, Dimensions.base(Time {}), "s").try
let kilometers = meters.scaled(1000.0, "km").try
let hours = seconds.scaled(3600.0, "h").try
let speed = (measure(36.0, kilometers) / measure(1.0, hours)).try
speed.convertTo((meters / seconds).try).try.value   # => 10.0
speed.convertTo(meters).ok?                         # => false
```

SI units such as metres, grams, watts and volts, with prefixes and dimensional arithmetic.

Nothing here is in scope until `using Units.SI`.

```kex
using Units.SI

main do
  IO.printLine(3.kilowatt.to(String))           # prints: 3.0 kW
  IO.printLine(5000.meter.to(String, in: Kilo(Meter)).or("")) # prints: 5.0 km
  IO.printLine((100.meter / 10.second).to(String)) # prints: 10.0 m/s
end
```

Every value is a prelude `Measure`, with its arithmetic, conversion and comparison. This module adds the SI unit names, including prefixed ones such as `kilometer`; the prefixes as units (`Kilo(Meter)`) for `convertTo` and `to(String, in:)`; and the dimension of each product and quotient, so `2.newton * 3.meter` is in joules and `100.meter / 10.second` in metres per second.
